description: def, arguments, return, and scope — package your code into reusable blocks.

screens.body:
A function is a named chunk of code you can run whenever you want. Define it once with def, then call it by name as many times as you like.

Without functions, you'd copy-paste the same code everywhere. With them, one fix updates every use — that's the whole game.

options: Runs the code inside def greet
check.question: What does calling greet() do?

screens.heading: Why functions exist
screens.keyPoint: def names a reusable block; calling it runs the block.

screens.body:
Functions get more useful when they accept inputs. The names in the def line are parameters — the slots. The values you pass when calling are arguments — what fills the slots.

People mix these words up constantly. Parameter = the placeholder in the definition. Argument = the real value in the call.
screens.heading: Arguments in, via parameters
screens.keyPoint: Parameters receive; arguments are what you send.

screens.body:
return hands a value back to whoever called the function. The caller can store it, print it, or feed it into something else.

A function without return still runs — but it gives back a special value called None, Python's way of saying "nothing here".
screens.heading: return sends a value back
screens.keyPoint: return passes a value back; no return means None.

screens.body:
print and return do different jobs. print shows text on the screen for humans. return hands data back to your code for later use.

Beginner trap: a function that prints its answer can't be reused — you can't store what it computed. Return the value, then decide what to do with it.

code.snippet:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

total = add(3, 4)
print(total)

screens.heading: return vs print
screens.keyPoint: print displays; return delivers a value you can reuse.

screens.body:
You can give a parameter a default value, making that argument optional. Callers who skip it get the default; callers who pass a value override it.

Defaults go at the end of the parameter list. They're great for the "usually this" case — like a greeting that usually says "friend".
screens.heading: Default arguments

screens.body:
Variables created inside a function are local — they exist only while the function runs, then vanish. Code outside can't see them.

Variables at the top level of your file are global — visible everywhere, including inside functions. Rule of thumb: keep variables as local as you can; it prevents spooky interference.

options: gone — it only existed inside show
check.question: After show() runs, y is…

code.snippet:
x = 10

def show():
    y = 5
    print(x + y)

show()

screens.heading: Scope: where variables live
screens.keyPoint: Inside-function variables stay inside; top-level ones are visible everywhere.

screens.body:
Two habits of good functions: do one job, and name it honestly. calculate_total is a good name; do_stuff is not.

If you catch yourself writing "and" in a function name — like fetch_and_display — that's a hint it wants to be two functions.
screens.heading: Small functions, clear names
screens.keyPoint: One function, one job, honest name.

screens.body: The official tutorial's functions section (docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html#defining-functions) covers def, arguments, defaults, and return with more examples. Short, clear, and worth the read.
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: The official docs are your best next stop.
